Information since September points to a still-strong labor market and moderate growth, but the softness in business fixed investment and exports is notable: the investment literature (e.g., Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994) shows investment—especially inventory and capex—plays a central role in cyclical fluctuations and is sensitive to internal funds and credit conditions, so weakness here raises downside risks to real GDP. The FOMC’s rate cut to 1.50–1.75% and reduction in IOER are consistent with New Keynesian evidence (Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido) and VAR-based findings (Sims; Zha; B. Friedman) that monetary easing supports output and gradually lifts inflation when price stickiness and a liquidity effect operate, though low market-based inflation compensation and anchored expectations (Svensson; Cagan) imply a measured, not immediate, pass-through to inflation. Open-economy work (Lane; Engel) and trade links indicate external weakness can weigh on employment via net exports, reinforcing the case for accommodation. The Desk’s T-bill purchases and repo operations chiefly address reserve adequacy and money market frictions—mitigating implementation risks rather than signaling QE—so the overall tone is cautiously supportive but tempered by investment and inflation undershoots.
